Excessively means to a degree that goes beyond what is acceptable, normal, or needed.

The key idea is a threshold — an invisible line that marks "enough." When something crosses that line and keeps going far beyond it, you use excessively to describe it.

Think of it like filling a glass with water. Filling it to the top is normal. Filling it until water spills all over the table? That's filling it excessively.
What Kind of Word It Is

Excessively is an adverb, which means it describes how much — it adds extra information to adjectives, verbs, or other adverbs.

  • excessively hot → describes the adjective "hot"
  • excessively worried → describes the adjective "worried"
  • He drinks excessively → describes the verb "drinks"

Here's something important: excessively is not neutral. It carries a negative judgment. When you say something is excessive, you're quietly saying: "This is too much, and it's a problem."

Compare:

  • She worked very hard. → neutral, possibly admiring
  • She worked excessively hard. → implies it was unhealthy or unreasonable

So the word always signals disapproval, concern, or criticism — even when spoken calmly.

English has many words to say "a lot," and they exist on a scale:

a little → quite → very → extremely → excessively

But excessively is different from all the others. Very and extremely just mean "a great amount." Excessively means "so much that it has become a problem or is no longer justified." It's not just about intensity — it's about crossing a line.

  • It was very expensive. → high price, just stating a fact
  • It was extremely expensive. → even higher, still just a fact
  • It was excessively expensive. → so expensive that it was unreasonable, unfair, or unjustified

1. "The punishment was excessively harsh."
→ The punishment went far beyond what the crime deserved. It wasn't just strict — it was unreasonably, unjustifiably strict.

2. "She apologized excessively, even though it wasn't her fault."
→ She kept apologizing over and over, more than the situation called for. It became awkward or unnecessary.

3. "He excessively monitors his employees."
→ He watches and checks on them so often and so closely that it crosses into being controlling or intrusive.

4. "The movie was excessively long."
→ It wasn't just long — it was so long that it felt wasteful, tiring, or padded with unnecessary content.

5. "Don't excessively water the plant."
→ Don't give it more water than it needs; too much water will actually harm it.
The Two Things That Make Something "Excessive"

When you use excessively, you're always implying one (or both) of these:

  1. It goes beyond what is needed — more than the situation requires
  2. It causes harm or problems — the excess has negative consequences

Both ideas are often present at the same time.
Common Collocations (Words Frequently Used With It)

Excessively pairs naturally with many words. Here are common ones, grouped by category:

Emotions/Behavior:
excessively anxious, excessively cautious, excessively jealous, excessively critical, excessively shy, excessively polite, excessively controlling

Physical things:
excessively hot, excessively cold, excessively loud, excessively bright, excessively long, excessively large

Actions:
drink excessively, eat excessively, spend excessively, work excessively, worry excessively
How It Differs From Similar Words

WordWhat it means
Very / ExtremelyA large amount — no judgment, just degree
OverlyVery similar to excessively, but slightly softer and more informal (overly dramatic)
ExcessivelyBeyond the acceptable limit — stronger judgment, more formal

Overly and excessively are close cousins. In most sentences, they're interchangeable — but excessively feels stronger and more formal, and often implies a more serious problem.

  • She's overly sensitive. → mildly critical
  • She's excessively sensitive. → more seriously critical, implies it's causing real issues
One Sentence to Remember It Forever

Excessively = so much that it goes past the point of being okay.

Whenever you see or use this word, that idea is always at its heart.
